We're starting to leave the territory where you'd test an LLM by e.g. "create an svg of pelican on a bicycle". As one idea to generalize it, I was interested what Opus 5 would do if I gave it the first paragraph of the Lord of the Rings, a 1M token budget (~$10) and asked for three js render of it. Opus went off for ~2 hours and wrote 5500 lines of code that (procedurally) rendered the story. It's kind of janky but fun. But it's a bit mindboggling that the LLM has to place and orchestrate various polygon assets in (x,y,z) coordinates and write code that animates it all, and that it even does anything at all. I also like this kind of examples because no one in their right mind would ever spend the time to write something this custom but LLMs have all the stamina and patience in the world, so it's an example where we go from "no one would ever do this" to "sure, why not, it's ~free". There might be a lot more. But I'm excited about creating hyper custom worlds that you can imagine dropping players into, e.g. here to participate in the LoTR story as a spectator NPC, or one of the characters, or etc. Something like an ephemeral GTA of X on demand. Last thought is that the domain of worlds/games exposes a weakness in LLMs: they can't easily audit their work because they aren't able to efficiently and natively perceive videos or play games within them. Here, Opus 5 had to very slowly and painstakingly take screenshots at different points, and it messed up a few times and created a bunch of jank. An example of raw capability (multimodal, gameplay) that I think is still quite lacking. Video

One pattern I find useful for working with LLMs is a nice long ramble session. Sometimes the LLM needs more bits to understand what you're trying to achieve, but you're too lazy to type them. In these cases I like to lean back, switch to /voice and just ramble for like 10 minutes, total mess, anything goes, full stream of consciousness. Sometimes I declare it up top, something like "switching to speech recognition sorry for any typos...". Sometimes I turn it into a small interview of a few turns. But I find that the LLMs are somehow very good at reconstructing long incoherent rambles and often their echo of your own tangle of thoughts comes out quite a bit cleaner than what you started with. The result is that you improve the mind meld and have to correct things less from that point on.

MiMo-V2.6 is "simply" the best (for now). Despite its simple architecture design it's currently No.1 in the open-weight benchmarks (weighted average). With "simple," I mean a classic Grouped Query Attention (GQA) with Sliding Window Attention (SWA) at a tiny 128-token window size. So, that underlines one of the points I've been trying to make in recent months: most of the progress still comes from the data and post-training recipe improvements. Fancy attention variants are just mostly efficiency tweaks. What are some of the training data improvements and recipe improvements? The MiMo team shared a pretty detailed technical report. Lots to carefully digest there, but in short, there are a few things that stood out: 1. An increase in agent tasks; also training across different harnesses (the average DeepSWE pass@1 accuracy on held-out harnesses improved from approximately 50% -> 66%). 2. Better reward signals: they replaced a simple correctness verifier with an agentic grader that looks at the execution traces as well. 3. Large RL batches (1,568 prompts × 16 rollouts = 25,088 trajectories) and 2.7–3.7 billion training tokens per update (unclear, though, what the predecessor used). Interesting new insights into the old AdamW vs Muon debate: Muon seems to do better because it reduces memorization. Calc Consulting (@CalcCon) 𝗔𝗱𝗮𝗺𝗪 𝘃𝘀. 𝗠𝘂𝗼𝗻: α, 𝗢𝘃𝗲𝗿𝗳𝗶𝘁𝘁𝗶𝗻𝗴, 𝗮𝗻𝗱 𝗠𝗲𝗺𝗼𝗿𝗶𝘇𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻. A quick update on our WeightWatcher experiments comparing AdamW with the newer Muon optimizer. We trained a single-head nanoGPT model with both optimizers across five seeds. We then used WeightWatcher to study the weight-matrix spectra and several forms of memorization. The top plot shows the average raw α. AdamW produces relatively stable α values. Muon is much noisier. Its ESDs vary substantially across layers, which makes α harder to estimate reliably. But the average hides something important: 👉 Individual layers do fall below α = 2. Our spectral/RG theory predicts that this regime can be associated with pathological, example-specific learning. So we tested that prediction directly. We inserted random sequences into the training set and measured whether the model remembered them using exact extraction, token recall, teacher-forced recall, and canary exposure. The result was striking. • AdamW memorized the planted sequences strongly. Earlier in training it reached ~96% exact recall of 32-token canaries. • Muon strongly suppressed this kind of memorization. At 10,000 steps, teacher-forced recall was ~62% for AdamW versus <1% for Muon. There is also a surprise: some Muon layers have α < 2 as well. So α < 2 by itself is not sufficient to explain memorization. This is why we recommend examining individual WeightWatcher layers and their ESDs—not simply average α. Muon appears to suppress memorization while also producing unusual ESDs that make conventional WeightWatcher analysis more difficult. We are now running Muon much longer to understand how these spectra evolve. tips.text_fr: Une méthode que je trouve utile pour travailler avec les LLM est une longue session de monologue. Parfois, le LLM a besoin de plus d'informations pour comprendre ce que vous essayez d'accomplir, mais vous êtes trop paresseux pour les taper. Dans ces cas, j'aime me pencher en arrière, passer en mode /voix et juste divaguer pendant environ 10 minutes, un désordre total, tout est permis, flux de conscience complet. Parfois, je le déclare en haut, quelque chose comme "passage à la reconnaissance vocale désolé pour les fautes de frappe...". Parfois, j'en fais une petite interview en quelques tours. Mais je trouve que les LLM sont d'une manière ou d'une autre très bons pour reconstruire de longs monologues incohérents et souvent leur écho de vos propres pensées confuses sort un peu plus clairement que ce avec quoi vous avez commencé. Le résultat est que vous améliorez la connexion mentale et que vous avez moins de choses à corriger à partir de ce moment-là.
tips.text_original: One pattern I find useful for working with LLMs is a nice long ramble session. Sometimes the LLM needs more bits to understand what you're trying to achieve, but you're too lazy to type them. In these cases I like to lean back, switch to /voice and just ramble for like 10 minutes, total mess, anything goes, full stream of consciousness. Sometimes I declare it up top, something like "switching to speech recognition sorry for any typos...". Sometimes I turn it into a small interview of a few turns. But I find that the LLMs are somehow very good at reconstructing long incoherent rambles and often their echo of your own tangle of thoughts comes out quite a bit cleaner than what you started with. The result is that you improve the mind meld and have to correct things less from that point on.

idees.text_fr: Nouvelles perspectives intéressantes sur le vieux débat AdamW vs Muon : Muon semble donner de meilleurs résultats car il réduit la mémorisation. Calc Consulting (@CalcCon) AdamW v.s. Muon : α, Overfitting, et Mémorisation. Une mise à jour rapide sur nos expériences WeightWatcher comparant AdamW avec le nouvel optimiseur Muon. Nous avons entraîné un modèle nanoGPT à tête unique avec les deux optimiseurs sur cinq graines. Nous avons ensuite utilisé WeightWatcher pour étudier le spectre de la matrice de poids et plusieurs formes de mémorisation. Le graphique supérieur montre la moyenne brute de α. AdamW produit des valeurs de α relativement stables. Muon est beaucoup plus bruyant. Ses ESD varient considérablement d'une couche à l'autre, ce qui rend l'estimation de α plus difficile de manière fiable. Mais la moyenne cache quelque chose d'important : 👉 Les couches individuelles tombent en dessous de α = 2. Notre théorie spectrale/RG prédit que ce régime peut être associé à un apprentissage pathologique spécifique à des exemples. Nous avons donc testé cette prédiction directement. Nous avons inséré des séquences aléatoires dans l'ensemble d'entraînement et mesuré si le modèle s'en souvenait en utilisant l'extraction exacte, le rappel de tokens, le rappel forcé par l'enseignant et l'exposition de canaris. Le résultat a été frappant. • AdamW a fortement mémorisé les séquences plantées. Plus tôt dans l'entraînement, il a atteint ~96 % de rappel exact de canaris de 32 tokens. • Muon a fortement supprimé ce type de mémorisation. À 10 000 étapes, le rappel forcé par l'enseignant était de ~62 % pour AdamW contre <1 % pour Muon. Il y a aussi une surprise : certaines couches Muon ont également α < 2. Donc α < 2 par lui-même n'est pas suffisant pour expliquer la mémorisation. C'est pourquoi nous recommandons d'examiner les couches individuelles de WeightWatcher et leurs ESD, et pas seulement la moyenne de α. Muon semble supprimer la mémorisation tout en produisant des ESD inhabituels qui rendent l'analyse conventionnelle de WeightWatcher plus difficile. Nous entraînons Muon beaucoup plus longtemps pour comprendre comment ces spectres évoluent. outils.text_fr: Si vous avez essayé hyperframes, vous sauriez que la pile vidéo agentique est construite sur la génération de code, mais le code SWE-bench vs la vidéo codée qui semble vivante sont deux choses différentes. Nous avons construit le Code2Video Bench, en collaboration avec Google DeepMind et @Kaggle. Frontier Labs peut enfin devenir bon dans les tâches vidéo agentiques. Vidéo
outils.text_original: if you tried hyperframes, you would know the agentic video stack is being built on code-gen but SWE-bench code v.s. code-to-video that feels alive are two different things we built the Code2Video Bench, in collab w/ Google DeepMind & @Kaggle frontier labs can finally get good at agentic video tasks Video
outils.decryptage: Le 'Code2Video Bench' est un nouvel outil créé par HyperFrames, Google DeepMind et Kaggle, conçu pour évaluer et améliorer la capacité des IA à générer des vidéos à partir de code, une étape clé vers des robots plus autonomes.
